The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
# Solving the GCD/LCM Operation Problem

## Key Insight: Prime Exponent Preservation

For each prime $p$, the multiset of $p$-exponents across all 2100 numbers is **invariant** under the operation, since $\nu_p(\gcd(a,b)) = \min(\nu_p(a), \nu_p(b))$ and $\nu_p(\text{lcm}(a,b)) = \max(\nu_p(a), \nu_p(b))$, and $\{\min, \max\}$ is just a reordering of $\{a, b\}$'s exponents.

Mark stops when no move changes the board, i.e., when for every pair, one number divides the other — the numbers form a **chain under divisibility**: $n_1 \mid n_2 \mid \cdots \mid n_{2100}$.

## Determining the Final Chain

In the chain, for each prime $p$, the exponents must be **non-decreasing**. Since the multiset of $p$-exponents is fixed, the $p$-exponent of the $i$-th smallest number is uniquely determined:

$$r_p(i) = k \iff 2100 - \left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^k} \right\rfloor < i \leq 2100 - \left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^{k+1}} \right\rfloor$$

## Computing $r_p(2026)$ for Each Prime

The condition simplifies to: $r_p(2026) = k \iff p^k \leq 28 < p^{k+1}$ (since $2100 - 2026 = 74$).

| Prime $p$ | $p^k \leq 28 < p^{k+1}$ | Exponent $r_p(2026)$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | $2^4 = 16 \leq 28 < 32 = 2^5$ | 4 |
| 3 | $3^3 = 27 \leq 28 < 81 = 3^4$ | 3 |
| 5 | $5^2 = 25 \leq 28 < 125 = 5^3$ | 2 |
| 7 | $7^1 = 7 \leq 28 < 49 = 7^2$ | 1 |
| 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 | $p^1 \leq 28 < p^2$ | 1 |
| $p \geq 29$ | $1 \leq 28 < p$ | 0 |

## Computing the Number of Divisors

The 2026th smallest number is:
$$N = 2^4 \cdot 3^3 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 7^1 \cdot 11^1 \cdot 13^1 \cdot 17^1 \cdot 19^1 \cdot 23^1$$

The number of positive divisors is:
$$\tau(N) = (4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6 = 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2^6 = 60 \cdot 64 = 3840$$

$$\boxed{3840}$$
